title: Checkout & Payment — end to end
subtitle: Cart to confirmation for a consumer e-commerce app, including the failures that actually happen
description:
Checkout is the shortest, most expensive screen flow a consumer product owns. Every extra field costs conversion, every unexplained failure costs the whole order, and the failure paths — a declined card, a 3-D Secure challenge, an address the carrier will not accept, a size that sells out while the shopper is typing their CVV — are not edge cases. On a healthy storefront roughly **one in seven checkout attempts** takes a non-happy path at least once, and the difference between a good checkout and a bad one is almost entirely in how those seven percent are handled.

This document draws three linked workflows.

1. **Checkout flow** (`ui`) is what the shopper sees: cart review, identification, address, delivery, payment method, authorization, confirmation. Each step carries a wireframe of the screen, the doors out of it, the empty/loading/error variants, and the literal microcopy.
2. **Payment authorization** (`data`) is the server-side span between the shopper tapping **Pay** and the word *authorized* — idempotency, fraud scoring, network tokenization, 3-D Secure step-up, retry on timeout, and the decline-code mapping that decides what the shopper is told.
3. **Recover abandoned** (`ops`) is what the business does when the first two never reach confirmation.

The three diagrams cross-reference each other. Checkout *inserts* payment authorization rather than duplicating it; payment authorization sends hard declines back to the payment-method step; both send dead carts to recovery.

> **Design stance taken throughout:** never blame the shopper, never lose typed data, and never show a payment error without showing the next action in the same viewport.

meta.source: Reconstructed from the checkout funnel spec, the PSP integration guide, and six months of decline-code telemetry

glossary.definition: A **hold** placed on the shopper's funds by the issuing bank, confirming the money exists and reserving it. It is not a charge. Capture — the actual movement of money — happens later, normally at ship time. An authorization typically expires in 7 days for cards and can be reversed instantly with a *void*.

The issuer-run challenge that shifts liability for a fraudulent transaction from the merchant to the bank. Under **SCA** rules it is mandatory for most EEA/UK consumer card payments unless an exemption applies. In 3DS2 the majority of transactions are *frictionless* — the issuer approves on device and network signals alone and the shopper never sees a challenge. When a challenge does fire it is an issuer-controlled sheet (biometric, app approval, or one-time passcode), not our UI.

A **soft** decline (`65`, `1A`, insufficient-funds-retryable, do-not-honor-with-step-up) means *try again differently* — usually with 3DS attached. A **hard** decline (`14` invalid number, `41` lost card, `43` stolen card, `54` expired) means *this card will never work*; retrying it is card-testing behaviour and gets the merchant rate-limited by the network.

A client-generated UUID sent with the authorization request so that a retry — after a timeout, a double-tap, or a mobile network flap — cannot create a second hold on the same card. The PSP stores the first response against the key and replays it verbatim for 24 hours.

**A**ddress **V**erification **S**ervice compares the numeric parts of the billing address (street number and postcode) with what the issuer has on file; CVV checks the 3-digit code. Results arrive as letter codes (`Y`, `A`, `Z`, `N`, `U`) and feed the risk decision. A full AVS match plus a CVV match is the single strongest low-risk signal available before the authorization returns.

A soft, time-boxed claim on stock — 20 minutes in this system — taken when checkout begins so a shopper mid-flow is not outbid by a faster one. It is *soft*: oversell protection is enforced again at authorization time, which is why a cart can still lose an item at the last second.

A cart with at least one line item, no completed order, and no shopper activity for 45 minutes. The quiet period matters — firing recovery too early reaches people who are still checking out and reads as surveillance.

Completing an order without creating an account. It measurably outperforms forced registration, so it is the primary path here; account creation is offered *after* the order is placed, when the shopper already has a password-worthy reason to say yes.

steps.title: Review the cart
steps.note: Last chance to see everything at once

detail.purpose: Give the shopper one honest, complete view of what they are about to buy before any commitment is asked of them. Every unpriced surprise later in the flow — shipping, tax, a duty estimate — costs more conversion here than the number itself ever would.

inputs.label: Line items
inputs.value: 1–40 SKUs with quantity, variant, unit price

inputs.label: Promotions
inputs.value: Auto-applied codes and any manually entered code

outputs.label: Reservation
outputs.value: 20-minute soft hold placed on every line

outputs.label: Estimate
outputs.value: Subtotal, shipping estimate, tax estimate, total

procedure: Re-price the cart server-side on load — never trust the price cached in the client, and never let a stale price render even for a frame.
Take a **20-minute soft inventory reservation** on every line and start a visible countdown only if the reservation is contested (someone else is holding the same last unit).
Render the estimated total *including* shipping and tax before the shopper commits to anything, using the coarsest geo signal available (IP or last known postcode).
Expose quantity steppers and a remove control inline; a shopper who has to leave checkout to fix the cart usually does not come back.
Show the promo-code field **collapsed** behind a text link. An open, empty promo field is one of the most reliable ways to send a shopper to a coupon site and lose the session.
rules: Estimated totals must be labelled *estimated* until the address is known. Silently changing a total after the shopper has read it is the single most cited reason for abandonment in our exit survey (31%).
Never auto-remove an out-of-stock line. Mark it, disable it, and let the shopper decide — auto-removal reads as the store deciding what they may buy.
The reservation is soft and advisory. Do not tell the shopper the item is *held for you* in language stronger than the guarantee we can actually keep.
Free-shipping progress (`£12 away from free delivery`) is shown only when the gap is under 25% of subtotal; above that it reads as an upsell, not help.

failureModes.then: Show the old and new price side by side with a one-line reason; do not silently re-price

failureModes.then: Disable the line, offer the nearest in-stock variant
Fail open — allow checkout, accept the oversell risk, alert ops

states.description: No line items. Show a single illustration, a one-line prompt, and two entry points: *Continue shopping* and *Recently viewed*. Never show a disabled checkout button on an empty cart — it implies the shopper did something wrong.

states.name: Loading
states.description: Skeleton rows sized to the last known line count so the layout does not jump. Totals render last and animate in; a total that flickers between two values reads as a pricing trick.

steps.title: Is every line still purchasable?
steps.note: Re-checked against live stock at checkout entry

detail.purpose: Catch stock and price drift at the *entry* to checkout rather than at the exit, where it is far more expensive. A shopper told about a sold-out size on the cart screen edits their order; a shopper told after their card is authorized files a complaint.

outputs.label: Availability map
outputs.value: `available` \| `partial` \| `unavailable` per line

procedure: Call inventory with the full line set in one request; per-line requests produce a visible staggered re-render that looks like the page is breaking.
Classify each line: fully available, partially available (requested 3, 1 left), or unavailable in this variant.
If everything is available, continue silently — **never** show a *Good news, everything is in stock!* interstitial. Confirming the absence of a problem creates the impression there was one.
If anything is short, surface it on the cart itself with the affected line highlighted and focus moved to it.
rules: The primary answer must be the successful one, so this question is phrased positively — *is everything purchasable*, not *is anything missing*.
A partial shortage is a quantity edit, not a removal; a total shortage is a removal decision the shopper must make.
Timeouts fail open. Losing an order to a slow inventory call is worse than the rare oversell, which is recoverable with an apology and a refund.
Do not re-run this check on every keystroke elsewhere in the flow; it runs here and again inside authorization, nowhere in between.

failureModes.then: Treat as available, tag the order `oversell-risk`, and let authorization catch it
Offer the reduced quantity as a one-tap edit
Offer the nearest sibling variant, then removal

procedure: Set the stepper to the maximum available quantity but do **not** commit it — the shopper taps to accept.
Recompute subtotal, any quantity-break discount, and free-delivery progress live as the number changes.

detail.purpose: Handle the one genuinely bad outcome on the cart screen without letting it end the session. A sold-out item is a reason to change the order, not a reason to leave the store.
procedure: Dim the line, strike the price, and keep it visible — deleting it outright makes the shopper wonder what changed.
Fetch up to three alternatives ranked by *same silhouette, same price band, in stock in this size*, in that order. Colour is the most acceptable substitution; size is the least.
Offer back-in-stock notification as a secondary action with a pre-filled email if we have one.
Send the shopper back to the top of the cart so they re-read the revised order before continuing.
rules: Never substitute automatically, even for an identical SKU in another colour.
If the sold-out line was the only line, do not dump the shopper on an empty cart — show alternatives on the cart itself.
Do not apologise more than once. A second apology in the same screen reads as evasion.

steps.title: Choose how to check out
steps.note: Guest is the default and the primary path

detail.purpose: Ask for the minimum identity we need to fulfil an order — an email address — while making account creation genuinely optional. Forced registration is the highest-cost gate in any checkout, and the account it produces is usually abandoned.

inputs.label: Email
inputs.value: Required in every branch — it is the order receipt address

inputs.label: Session hints
inputs.value: Existing auth cookie, saved credential from the browser, wallet identity

outputs.label: Identity
outputs.value: `guest` \| `authenticated` \| `new-account`

outputs.label: Prefill set
outputs.value: Saved addresses and payment instruments, when authenticated

procedure: Lead with the email field, focused, keyboard set to `email`, autocomplete `email` — not with a choice of three tabs. The field is common to every path, so asking for it first makes the fork feel smaller than it is.
Detect a returning shopper from the entered email *after blur*, and offer sign-in inline: `You have an account — sign in to use your saved details?` Never block on it.
Run typo correction on common domains (`gmial`, `hotmial`, `yaho`) and offer the correction as a tappable suggestion, never an auto-fix.
Surface platform credential managers and wallets (Apple Pay, Google Pay, passkeys) above the fold — a wallet identity supplies email, address, and payment in one gesture and skips three screens.
Place account creation *after* the fork as a low-emphasis option, and repeat the offer on the confirmation screen where it converts roughly four times better.
rules: Guest must be the visually primary option. If both look equal, shoppers read the account option as required.
Never say *Register* or *Create your account to continue*. The word *continue* must never be attached to a gate.
Email is validated for syntax and MX only — never for deliverability inline, which is too slow and produces false rejections.
A signed-in shopper skips address entry only if the saved address passed validation on a previous order; otherwise it is re-verified.
Marketing consent is a separate, unticked checkbox with its own label. It is never bundled into the order-placement action.

failureModes.then: Inline error under the field on blur, never on keystroke
Offer guest checkout with the same email rather than a lockout dead end
Return to this step with the email preserved

options.label: Continue as guest
options.why: Primary because it is both the most-taken and the cheapest path. Guest checkout removes the password decision entirely, and a password decision inside checkout is a context switch the shopper's working memory cannot afford while holding a cart total.

options.label: Sign in
options.why: Offered second because for returning shoppers it is *faster* than guest — saved address and saved card can collapse three screens into one. The pitch is speed, not loyalty.

options.label: Create an account
options.why: Lowest emphasis and deliberately so. It is here only for shoppers who arrived intending to register; everyone else gets the same offer post-order, when the account has visible value (tracking, returns) and costs no momentum.

steps.title: Authenticate the returning shopper
steps.note: Passkey first, password second

detail.purpose: Get a returning shopper back to their saved address and card in as few gestures as possible, without turning a failed password into a lost order.
detail.duration: 5–20 s with a passkey, 25–60 s with a password reset

inputs.label: Email
inputs.value: Carried forward from the previous step, read-only

outputs.label: Session
outputs.value: Short-lived checkout-scoped token, 30 min TTL

procedure: Carry the email forward as read-only text with an `Edit` affordance. Re-typing an email you just typed is the most irritating regression in any sign-in panel.
Attempt a passkey assertion automatically on load where one is registered — for most returning shoppers this resolves in a single biometric prompt.
Fall back to password with a visible `Show` toggle and the field typed `current-password` for the credential manager.
Offer a **magic link** as the third option before offering a password reset; resets destroy checkout sessions.
Rate-limit at five attempts per email per fifteen minutes, and on the fourth attempt proactively surface guest checkout with the same email.
rules: Never lock a shopper out mid-checkout. The escape hatch is always guest checkout, never a dead end.
Do not require a captcha before the third failed attempt — the friction cost on legitimate shoppers exceeds the bot cost at this volume.
The panel is a sheet over the checkout, not a navigation. Dismissing it returns to the fork with all typed data intact.

failureModes.when: Passkey assertion fails or is cancelled
failureModes.then: Fall through to password silently, no error
Offer magic link, then guest checkout
Offer guest checkout without explaining the lock

steps.note: Only verified, non-expired records

assign.name: shopper.addresses
assign.value: Saved addresses where `verifiedAt` is not null

assign.value: Network tokens not expired within 30 days

detail.purpose: Populate the rest of checkout from the profile so the returning shopper can potentially skip two entire screens — but only with data we still trust.

outputs.value: 0–8 verified addresses, default first

outputs.value: 0–5 network tokens with last4, brand, expiry

procedure: Filter out addresses that have never passed validation, and any address whose last delivery attempt failed.
Filter out instruments expiring within 30 days — an expired card discovered at authorization is a decline the shopper reads as our fault.
Order addresses by *most recent successful delivery*, not by creation date. Recency of success is a far better predictor than recency of entry.
Mask everything: `•••• 4242`, `221B Baker St, NW1 …`. Never render a full PAN or a full address string in a summary row.
Set `checkout.prefilled` so downstream steps can render *confirm* affordances rather than *enter* affordances.
rules: Prefill is a suggestion, never a commitment. Every prefilled value must be one tap from being changed.
Never prefill an instrument that has produced a hard decline in the last 60 days.
Shared-device risk: if the session is on a device flagged as shared, mask more aggressively and require re-entry of CVV.

failureModes.then: Continue as if no saved data exists; do not block

failureModes.when: All saved addresses fail the verified filter

detail.purpose: Convert the value of having an account into an actual saved screen. A signed-in shopper with a previously validated address has already told us everything the address step would ask, so asking again is pure friction.

Preserve the choice in the session so a later back-navigation does not re-ask.

steps.note: One field, no profile questions

detail.purpose: Let shoppers who *want* an account create one in a single gesture, without turning checkout into a registration form.

outputs.label: Account
outputs.value: Created in `pending` state, promoted on order placement

procedure: Ask for exactly one thing: a credential. No name, no phone, no marketing preferences, no date of birth — the address step supplies the name and everything else can be asked later or never.
Offer passkey creation first; it is faster, has no strength rules to explain, and cannot be forgotten.

Create the account in a `pending` state and promote it only when the order is placed. An abandoned checkout must not leave a half-account that blocks the same email from checking out as a guest tomorrow.
State the benefit in one line at the top — order tracking and one-tap returns — and do not sell any further.
rules: No password strength meter with rejection rules inside checkout. Enforce a length minimum and a breach-list check; reject nothing else.
Marketing consent is a separate unticked box and never a precondition.
If account creation fails for any reason, the order continues as a guest order. The order is never held hostage to the account.

steps.title: Enter the delivery address
steps.note: Autocomplete first, manual fields as fallback

detail.purpose: Collect a deliverable address with the fewest keystrokes and the least opportunity to make a mistake the carrier will punish later. Address entry is the longest-dwell screen in checkout and the one where mobile shoppers give up most often.
detail.actor: Shopper, assisted by an autocomplete provider

inputs.label: Partial address string
inputs.value: Typed into a single search field

inputs.label: Geo hint
inputs.value: Country from locale, biasing autocomplete results

inputs.label: Prefill
inputs.value: Platform autofill or saved profile, where available

outputs.label: Structured address
outputs.value: `{name, line1, line2, city, region, postcode, country}`

outputs.label: Address entry mode
outputs.value: `autocomplete` \| `manual` — tracked, because manual correlates with delivery failure

procedure: Open with a **single search field**, not a seven-field form. `Start typing your address` resolves most UK and US addresses in four or five characters.

procedure: POST the authorization request with the idempotency key and wait. The client does not poll — it holds an open request with a 30-second timeout.

Never allow back-navigation or a second submit while the request is open. The idempotency key makes a duplicate harmless, but the UI should not invite one.

On timeout, do **not** assume failure. Query the authorization by idempotency key before telling the shopper anything — a timeout with a successful authorization behind it is how double charges are born.

Reject any currency that is not the order's currency; there is no conversion at authorization time.
Attach a trace id and start the 25-second server budget clock — five seconds inside the client's 30-second timeout, so the client always outlives us and can resolve state.
rules: Amount is authoritative from the order, never from the request body.
Requests older than 15 minutes by their `Date` header are rejected as replayed.
The payment token is single-use and must be unused; a reused token is a `409`, not a retry.

steps.title: Is this idempotency key unseen?
steps.note: The double-charge firewall

detail.purpose: Guarantee that a retry — from a double tap, a flaky mobile network, or a client timeout — can never create a second hold on the shopper's card. This single check is the difference between a payment system people trust and one they do not.

outputs.label: Verdict
outputs.value: `new` \| `in_flight` \| `completed`

outputs.label: Lock
outputs.value: 30-second Redis lock on `new`, renewed while processing

procedure: `SET key … NX PX 30000` in Redis. Success means this is the first request for the key and we hold the lock.
On failure, read `payment_attempts` by key: a row with a terminal status is `completed`; no terminal row means `in_flight`.
Compare the stored request fingerprint with this request's. A same key with a *different* body is a client bug and returns `422`, never a replay of an unrelated response.
On `completed`, replay the stored response verbatim — same status code, same body, same auth code. Recomputing anything defeats the guarantee.
On `in_flight`, return `409 in_flight` with a `Retry-After`; the client waits rather than issuing a competing request.
Persist the response against the key with a 24-hour TTL as the last act of every terminal path.
rules: Keys are scoped to `(merchant, key)` and live 24 hours. Beyond that a retry is a new transaction and the client must mint a new key.
Same key + different body is always a `422`. Silently replaying would return the wrong order's auth code.
The lock is renewed every 10 seconds while processing so a slow issuer cannot cause a competing attempt.
Redis is a fast path, not the source of truth. If Redis is unavailable, fall back to a Postgres unique-constraint insert — slower, still correct.

failureModes.then: Fall back to a unique insert on `payment_attempts`; latency rises, correctness holds
The unique constraint still blocks a second insert; the competing request gets `in_flight`
`422 idempotency_key_reuse` — a client bug, surfaced loudly

schema.note: Canonicalised body; guards against key reuse

INSERT INTO payment_attempts (key, request_hash, status, expires_at)
VALUES ($1, $2, 'in_flight', now() + interval '24 hours')
ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING
RETURNING key;
-- zero rows returned => someone else owns this key
```

steps.note: No second hold is ever attempted

detail.purpose: Tell a duplicate request to wait rather than competing, so a double tap or a reconnect never produces two authorizations.

procedure: Return `409` with a `Retry-After` derived from how long the original attempt has been running — typically 2 seconds, never more than 5.

Do not queue, do not block, do not proxy the original response. The client polls; the server stays stateless.
Emit a `payment.duplicate_suppressed` metric — a rising rate is usually a client-side double-submit bug worth fixing at the source.
rules: Never attempt a second authorization for an in-flight key, under any circumstances.
`Retry-After` is advisory but the client honours it; ignoring it produces a thundering herd on a slow issuer.
The shopper must never see this state — the client absorbs it silently under the existing waiting UI.

steps.title: Assemble the authorization request
steps.note: Amount, descriptor, MIT flags, exemptions

detail.purpose: Turn an internal order into a processor-shaped authorization request, making the small decisions — descriptor text, capture method, exemption claims — that measurably change both approval rate and chargeback volume.

inputs.label: Order
inputs.value: Total, currency, line count, shipping country

inputs.label: Shopper history
inputs.value: Prior successful orders on this instrument

outputs.label: Authorization request
outputs.value: PSP-shaped payload, not yet sent

procedure: Re-derive the amount from the order one final time. Every layer that can re-derive, does.
Build the statement descriptor to include the **order number**. A descriptor a shopper cannot connect to a purchase is the leading cause of *I don't recognise this charge* chargebacks.
Set `capture_method: manual`. We authorize at checkout and capture at dispatch, because capturing before shipping is both a refund liability and, in several jurisdictions, non-compliant.

Evaluate SCA exemptions: low-value under £30 (with the cumulative counter respected), or trusted-beneficiary where the shopper has previously allow-listed us. A valid exemption skips the 3DS challenge entirely and lifts conversion on this segment by around six points.
Mark the transaction customer-initiated. Mis-flagging a CIT as merchant-initiated is a common source of unexplained declines.
Attach the network token rather than the PAN wherever one exists; token authorizations approve at a measurably higher rate and survive card reissue.
rules: Never claim an exemption we cannot evidence. A challenged exemption that fails costs the liability shift and the transaction.
Descriptor is capped at 22 characters by most networks; truncation must preserve the order number, not the brand.
Capture is never automatic, for any order type, including digital goods.
The amount in the request must equal the amount on the order review screen the shopper approved. No fees are added here.

steps.title: Score risk and resolve the token concurrently
steps.note: Three tracks, joined at 800 ms
tracks: Fraud score — device, velocity, behavioural signals
Network tokenization — resolve or refresh the DPAN
AVS/CVV preparation — normalise the billing address

detail.purpose: Run every independent pre-authorization computation at the same time, because they do not depend on each other and running them in sequence would add roughly 600 ms to every single checkout.
detail.duration: p50 240 ms · p95 780 ms · 800 ms deadline

inputs.label: Device signals
inputs.value: Fingerprint, IP reputation, session age, typing cadence

inputs.label: Velocity counters
inputs.value: Attempts per card, per device, per email, per hour

outputs.label: Risk score
outputs.value: 0–100 with contributing reason codes

outputs.label: Network token
outputs.value: DPAN plus cryptogram, or null

outputs.label: AVS payload
outputs.value: Numeric street and postcode components only

procedure: Fan out all three tracks with a shared 800 ms deadline. Whatever has not returned by then is treated as unavailable, not awaited.
**Fraud track:** submit the full signal set and take back a score with reason codes. Reason codes matter more than the score — they are what a human reviewer reads.
**Token track:** resolve the network token for the instrument, refreshing it if it is within 30 days of expiry. A refreshed token survives card reissue and quietly saves the shopper a re-entry later.

**AVS track:** reduce the billing address to the numeric components the networks actually compare — street number and postcode. Sending the full address adds nothing and occasionally causes mismatches on punctuation.
Join at the deadline and carry forward whatever arrived. Missing tracks degrade the decision; they never block it.
rules: The deadline is hard. A fraud engine that hangs must never hold a shopper's payment.
A missing fraud score is treated as the review band, not as low risk — fail closed on risk, open on latency.
A missing network token falls back to the PSP token; this costs a little approval rate and nothing else.
No track may mutate shared state; each returns a value and nothing more.

failureModes.then: Treat as review band, force 3DS step-up
Use the PSP token; refresh the network token out of band
Proceed with 3DS forced and no exemption claim

steps.note: < 40 clear · 40–79 review · >= 80 block

detail.purpose: Decide whether this attempt proceeds untouched, proceeds with a forced 3-D Secure step-up, or does not proceed at all. The thresholds are a business decision about the trade between fraud loss and false-positive loss, and false positives cost more.

inputs.value: High-value orders shift the review band down

outputs.label: Band
outputs.value: `clear` \| `review` \| `block`

outputs.label: Step-up requirement
outputs.value: Forces 3DS regardless of exemption when `review`

procedure: Apply the base bands: below 40 clear, 40 to 79 review, 80 and above block.
Shift the review threshold down to 30 for orders over £500 and for first-order-on-a-new-device.
Override to review — never to clear — on any hard reason code (`bin_country_mismatch`, `velocity_card_1h > 3`), whatever the numeric score says.
On review, drop any SCA exemption claim and force a 3DS challenge. A challenge is a far better answer to uncertainty than a refusal.
On block, record the decision with the full reason set and return a terminal failure. Blocked attempts are reviewed daily for false positives.
Never expose the band, the score or the reasons to the client. All three are useful to an attacker probing thresholds.
rules: A missing score is review, not clear. Latency must not become a fraud vector.
Block is rare by design — under 0.3% of attempts. A rising block rate is treated as an incident, not a success.
The shopper is never told they were blocked for risk; the copy is the ordinary decline message.
Thresholds are configuration, not code, and every change is recorded with an owner and a reason.

Treat as review

failureModes.then: Page the risk on-call; a bad rule usually ships just before this

Record the reason codes that produced the review band, so a false positive can be diagnosed without re-running the model.
Do not increase the amount, change the descriptor, or alter anything else about the request. The only change is the authentication posture.
Let the issuer decide the challenge shape. Some will still resolve frictionlessly on their own signals, which is the ideal outcome.

Never force a challenge on a merchant-initiated transaction; there is no cardholder present to answer it.
If the issuer does not support 3DS2, proceed without and accept the liability — refusing would lose an otherwise good order.

steps.title: Send the authorization to the processor
steps.note: One open request, 8 s timeout

detail.purpose: Actually ask the issuer for the money. Everything before this step was preparation; everything after is interpretation. This is the only call in the flow that can move value.
detail.actor: Payment service → PSP → card network → issuer
detail.duration: p50 1.4 s · p95 4.8 s · 8 s timeout

inputs.label: Idempotency key
inputs.value: Passed through to the PSP, which honours it independently

outputs.label: Processor response

outputs.value: Recorded per issuer BIN for routing decisions

procedure: POST to the PSP with our idempotency key. The PSP honours it independently of our own guard — two layers of the same protection, because the failure mode is unacceptable.
Set an 8-second timeout. Beyond that the shopper has almost certainly assumed failure and the issuer is unlikely to answer usefully.
Record the full response including AVS and CVV letter codes; they drive the decline explanation the shopper eventually reads.
Record latency keyed by issuer BIN. Slow issuers are a real, persistent, and routable phenomenon.
Never log the PAN, the cryptogram, or the CVV. Log the token reference, the last four, and nothing else.
Emit `payment.authorization_sent` before the call and the paired outcome event after, so a crash between them is visible rather than silent.
rules: Exactly one in-flight authorization per idempotency key. Enforced twice.
8-second timeout is fixed, not adaptive. An adaptive timeout makes incident behaviour unpredictable.
A timeout is **not** a decline. It is an unknown state and must be resolved by query, never by assumption.
PCI scope: the PAN never enters our process memory. We hold tokens only.

failureModes.then: Retry once with the same key after jittered backoff
Same retry path; 5xx is a network condition, not a decision
Map the code and stop; never retry

schema.note: Keyed by issuer BIN for routing

steps.title: Did the issuer approve on this attempt?
steps.note: Four outcomes; only one is terminal-bad

detail.purpose: Interpret the processor's answer correctly. Nearly every expensive payments bug lives in this step: treating a timeout as a decline, retrying a hard decline, or discarding an `attempted` authentication.

outputs.label: Route
outputs.value: Approved · step-up · retry · terminal decline

procedure: `succeeded` with issuer code `00` is approval. Continue to the oversell check.
`requires_action` means the issuer wants 3-D Secure. Hand the challenge URL back to the client and keep this attempt open server-side.
`timeout` or `5xx` is an **unknown** state. Retry once with the same idempotency key after jittered backoff, then query by key if the retry is also inconclusive.

`failed` with a hard code (`14`, `41`, `43`, `54`) is terminal. Map it and stop — never retry, because retrying hard declines is card-testing behaviour that gets a merchant rate-limited by the networks.
`failed` with a soft code (`65`, `1A`) is a request to re-attempt with 3DS attached, not a refusal.
Branch order here mirrors severity: step-up is recoverable in seconds, timeout in one retry, hard decline only by changing the instrument.
rules: A timeout is never a decline. This is the single most important rule in the workflow.
Maximum one automatic retry per idempotency key, ever.
Soft and hard declines are distinguished by table lookup, not by prefix heuristics.
Unknown issuer codes are treated as hard declines and logged for mapping within the week.

failureModes.then: Treat as hard decline, alert the payments team to map it
Query the PSP by idempotency key before deciding anything
Expire the attempt at 10 minutes and void any pending hold

steps.title: Resume authorization with the authentication value
steps.note: Same key, now carrying the CAVV

detail.purpose: Complete the authorization after the shopper has satisfied the issuer's challenge, attaching the authentication value that both proves the check happened and moves chargeback liability to the bank.
detail.actor: Payment service, after the client returns the challenge result

inputs.label: ECI
inputs.value: Electronic commerce indicator, evidences the liability shift

outputs.label: Final authorization
outputs.value: Approved or declined, with the 3DS data attached

outputs.label: Liability record
outputs.value: Stored for the chargeback file

procedure: Accept `Y` **and** `A` as success. `A` means *attempted* and still carries the liability shift; discarding it is a common and expensive integration bug.
Re-send the authorization with the same idempotency key, now including the CAVV and ECI.
Store the CAVV and ECI against the payment. Without them the liability shift cannot be evidenced when a chargeback arrives months later.
Treat `N` and `R` as authentication failure — terminal for this instrument, and never re-challenged in the same session.
Treat `U` as one exemption-based retry where the rules allow, then as failure.
A challenge that passes can still be declined for funds. Present that as an ordinary decline, never as an authentication problem.
rules: `A` is a success. Stated separately because it is the most frequently mis-implemented rule in 3DS2.
The idempotency key is unchanged across the challenge — this is one attempt, not two.
Never re-challenge the same card in the same session after `N` or `R`.
The 10-minute challenge window is enforced server-side; an expired challenge voids any pending hold.

failureModes.then: Terminal for this instrument; the client offers another method

failureModes.when: Authorization declines after a passed challenge
failureModes.then: Map as an ordinary decline; do not mention authentication
Void any pending hold and fail the attempt

branches.label: Timeout
branches.note: Unknown state — retry once with the same key

steps.title: Back off with jitter, then retry once
steps.note: Same idempotency key — never a second hold

detail.purpose: Recover from a network or processor blip without ever creating a second authorization. A timeout means we do not know what happened, and the only safe way to find out is to ask again with the same key.
detail.duration: 400–900 ms backoff, then a second 8 s attempt

inputs.label: Retry count
inputs.value: Must be 0; hard cap of one retry

inputs.label: Idempotency key
inputs.value: Unchanged — this is the entire safety mechanism

outputs.label: Second attempt result
outputs.value: Or a definitive query result if it is also inconclusive

procedure: Sleep for a jittered 400–900 ms. Fixed backoff across a fleet synchronises retries and turns a blip into an outage.
Re-send the identical request with the identical key. If the first attempt actually succeeded, the PSP replays that success rather than authorizing again.
If the retry also times out, stop retrying and **query** the PSP by idempotency key. Querying is cheap, safe, and definitive.
If the query is inconclusive, mark the attempt `unknown`, void defensively after 60 seconds, and page the payments on-call.
Never exceed one automatic retry. Beyond that, humans decide.
rules: Same key, always. A retry with a new key is a double charge waiting to happen.
Jitter is mandatory.
The client's 30-second budget must accommodate backoff plus a second 8-second attempt; it does, with margin.
An `unknown` attempt is voided defensively rather than left holding funds.

failureModes.then: Query by key; do not retry a third time
Treat as approved and continue normally
Mark `unknown`, void after 60 s, page on-call

{
  "retry_count": 1,
  "backoff_ms": 613,
  "resolution": "retry_succeeded",
  "idempotency_key": "8f14e45f-ea8b-4a2f-9d1c-5b1c2a7e0c31",
  "note": "PSP replayed the original success; no second hold created"
}
```

FROM authorization_retries

WHERE status = 'unknown'

branches.label: Hard decline
branches.note: Terminal for this instrument — never retried

steps.title: Map the issuer code to shopper-safe copy
steps.note: Nine messages, one per cause

detail.purpose: Translate a two-character network code into something a person can act on, without leaking anything useful to a card tester and without blaming the shopper.

inputs.label: AVS / CVV letters
inputs.value: Used to detect a typo rather than a refusal

outputs.label: Message key
outputs.value: One of nine; the client owns the wording

outputs.label: Suggested action
outputs.value: `different_card` · `check_details` · `wallet` · `contact_bank`

outputs.label: Reference id
outputs.value: Short, shopper-quotable, support-searchable

procedure: Look the code up in the mapping table. `05 do not honour` — the most common and least informative — maps to `bank_declined` with `different_card`.
Override to `check_details` when AVS is `N` or CVV is `N` on an otherwise benign code. This distinction recovers a meaningful share of declines that would otherwise be lost.
`54 expired card` maps to `card_expired` with `check_details`, and the client focuses the expiry field on return — the one decline with an obvious one-field fix.
`51 insufficient funds` maps to `insufficient_funds` with `different_card`. Never suggest waiting; the shopper knows their balance.
Return only the message key, never the raw code. The client owns the wording so copy can change without a backend deploy.
Mint a short reference id (`PA-7K2Q`) that support can search, and that a shopper can read aloud.
rules: Raw issuer codes never leave the payment service.
`contact_bank` is never a primary action — it is the slowest remedy and reads as a brush-off.
Unmapped codes fall back to `bank_declined` and raise a ticket; the mapping table is expected to be complete within a week of any new code appearing.
Decline copy never contains the words *rejected*, *invalid*, or *failed*.

failureModes.then: Generic `bank_declined`, log for mapping
Generic decline; the flow must not fail because copy selection failed

FROM declines
WHERE created_at > now() - interval '30 days'
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 3 DESC;

queries.code:
SELECT count(*) AS typo_declines,

FROM declines
WHERE suggested_action = 'check_details'

steps.title: Is every line still in stock?
steps.note: The authoritative check — reservations are advisory

detail.purpose: Perform the one inventory check that is actually binding, at the last possible moment before the order becomes real. Everything earlier was a soft reservation; this is the decrement that either succeeds or does not.

inputs.label: Authorization
inputs.value: Already held — this is why order matters here

outputs.label: Decrement result
outputs.value: Per line: `committed` or `conflict`

outputs.label: Commitment
outputs.value: Stock moved from reserved to committed on success

procedure: Run a single atomic multi-line decrement. Per-line decrements can partially succeed and leave the order in a state nobody can reason about.
Compare against *available* stock, not reserved — the shopper's own reservation is excluded from the contention it would otherwise create with itself.
On success, move the lines from reserved to committed and release the soft reservation.
On conflict, do not commit anything. Void the authorization and hand the whole situation to the checkout client, which owns the apology.
Record the reservation id and the winning order on every conflict, so the inventory team can find the race rather than guess at it.
rules: This check runs **after** authorization, not before. Authorizing first and checking second means a rare void; checking first and authorizing second means a common oversell.
Never partially commit. All lines or none.
A conflict is our failure, not the shopper's, and every downstream message must reflect that.
Oversell rate above 1% for any SKU triggers a buffer adjustment on that SKU.

failureModes.then: Void the whole authorization; the client offers partial fulfilment
Commit optimistically and flag for dispatch review — the order is already paid for
Query commitment state by reservation id before deciding

schema.note: Which order took the last unit — for race analysis

queries.label: Oversell conflicts by SKU

FROM inventory_conflicts
WHERE ts > now() - interval '30 days'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 20;

queries.label: Conflict rate against reservation age

       count(*) FILTER (WHERE result = 'conflict')::float / count(*) AS conflict_rate
FROM inventory_commits
WHERE ts > now() - interval '14 days'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

steps.title: Void the hold before anyone is told
steps.note: Money released first, explanation second

detail.purpose: Release the shopper's money the instant we know we cannot ship, so that every subsequent message can truthfully say nothing was taken.

inputs.label: Conflict detail
inputs.value: Which SKUs, which reservation, which winning order

outputs.label: Void confirmation
outputs.value: Hold released; statement clears in 0–5 business days

outputs.label: Order state
outputs.value: `cancelled_oversell` with the conflict attached

procedure: Issue the void immediately, before writing the order state or emitting any event. The money is the shopper's and it comes first.
Retry the void with backoff for 60 seconds. If it still fails, escalate to a same-day refund and change the downstream copy to describe a refund rather than a released hold.
Release any gift-card hold in the same operation — a stranded stored-value hold is the worst support ticket in the flow.
Set the order to `cancelled_oversell` with the conflicting SKUs attached, so care agents can see what happened without asking.
Emit `order.oversell_cancelled` for the recovery workflow and for the back-in-stock notification.
Auto-issue a goodwill credit for any express delivery paid; the shopper bought speed and we delivered nothing.
rules: Never capture funds for an order that cannot ship, even briefly.
The void must precede the shopper-facing message, always.
State fund-release timing honestly — instant on our side, up to five business days on a statement.
Do not count this against the shopper's decline or fraud counters in any way.

failureModes.when: Void fails after 60 s of retries
failureModes.then: Same-day refund; change the copy from *released* to *refunded*
Page ops immediately; stored value stranded is a hard support case
Void in full; the client offers a fresh partial order

schema.note: Express delivery paid, plus a fixed £10

steps.title: Persist the authorization and close the key
steps.note: One transaction, then the outbox

assign.name: payment.expires_at
assign.value: now() + 7 days — the hold's natural life

detail.purpose: Write the authoritative record of what happened, in one transaction, so that no crash after this point can lose the fact that the shopper's money is held.

inputs.label: Authorization result
inputs.value: Auth code, AVS/CVV letters, 3DS data if present

inputs.label: Idempotency key
inputs.value: To be closed with the frozen response

outputs.label: Payment row
outputs.value: `authorized`, with the full processor response

outputs.label: Order row
outputs.value: `confirmed`

outputs.label: Outbox rows
outputs.value: Events to be published after commit

procedure: Write the payment row, the order status change, and the idempotency response into **one** database transaction. Split writes here are how orders end up paid but not confirmed.
Freeze the response body against the idempotency key for 24-hour replay before the transaction commits.
Enqueue every downstream event to a transactional outbox rather than publishing inline. Publishing before commit is how a fulfilment system learns about an order that then rolls back.
Store the 3DS authentication data (CAVV, ECI, DS transaction id) with the payment — a chargeback arriving in four months needs it and cannot obtain it later.
Set the hold expiry to seven days and schedule the capture-or-void reconciliation job.
Never store the PAN, the cryptogram, or the CVV. Token reference and last four only.
rules: One transaction. No exceptions.
Outbox, never inline publish.
The idempotency response is frozen before commit, so a crash immediately after commit still replays correctly.
Payment rows are append-mostly; status transitions are recorded, never overwritten in place.

failureModes.when: Transaction fails after a successful authorization
failureModes.then: Reconciler finds the orphan hold by idempotency key within 60 s and either completes or voids it
Order is still confirmed; fulfilment catches up. Alert at 5 minutes of lag
Idempotent no-op; this is a replay racing the original

FROM payments

steps.title: Publish payment.authorized
steps.note: From the outbox, after commit

detail.purpose: Tell the rest of the business that this order is real, exactly once, and only after the database says so.

inputs.label: Outbox row
inputs.value: Topic and payload written inside the authorizing transaction

outputs.label: Event
outputs.value: `payment.authorized` on `payments.v2`, keyed by order id

outputs.label: Downstream effects
outputs.value: Fulfilment pick, confirmation email, conversion record

procedure: Poll the outbox, publish in commit order, and mark rows published only after the broker acknowledges.
Key the event by order id so all events for one order land on the same partition and consumers see them in order.
Include a schema version in the payload. Consumers that cannot read it must fail loudly rather than silently dropping fields.
Publish at-least-once and require consumers to be idempotent — exactly-once across a broker boundary is a comfortable fiction.
Fire the analytics conversion from this event, not from the confirmation page view. Page views are refreshed, closed and bot-visited; events are not.
rules: Nothing is published before commit, ever.
At-least-once delivery; consumers deduplicate on `event_id`.
No PII beyond the order and customer ids in the payload; consumers resolve details themselves.
Publisher lag over 5 minutes pages the on-call — it means orders exist that nobody is picking.

failureModes.then: Rows accumulate in the outbox and publish on recovery; order integrity is unaffected
Deduplication on `event_id` makes it a no-op

failureModes.when: Schema version unknown to a consumer
failureModes.then: Consumer halts its partition and alerts rather than dropping fields

workflows.title: Abandoned checkout recovery
workflows.description: The operational process that runs when a cart is created but no order follows. Detects abandonment after a quiet period, decides whether we are allowed to make contact, restores the cart, and hands the shopper back to checkout.

summary.trigger: No order and no cart activity for 45 minutes on a non-empty cart
summary.outcome: Shopper returns and completes, or the cart is closed cleanly with no further contact
summary.owner: Lifecycle marketing, with Platform on-call for the pipeline
summary.duration: 45 min to first email · 72 h to close

start.label: Cart goes quiet
start.note: Also entered directly from checkout on an oversell cancellation

steps.title: Detect the abandonment
steps.note: Stream job over cart and order events

detail.purpose: Identify carts that have genuinely been abandoned, as distinct from carts whose owner is still shopping, still checking out, or has already ordered on another device.
detail.duration: Continuous; decisions emitted within 60 s of the quiet threshold

outputs.label: Abandonment candidate
outputs.value: Cart id, customer key, last activity, furthest checkout step reached

runbook: The job keys by cart id and holds a 45-minute session window on last activity. Any cart event resets the window.
Suppress immediately on `order.confirmed` for the same customer key, even for a different cart — someone who ordered from another device has not abandoned anything.

Record the **furthest checkout step reached**. It is the strongest single predictor of recovery: shoppers who abandoned at payment recover at roughly three times the rate of those who abandoned at the cart.
Oversell cancellations enter here directly rather than waiting out the quiet period; the shopper has already been told, and the follow-up is a back-in-stock notice, not a nudge.
Watermark lateness is 5 minutes. Events later than that are dropped and counted, not reprocessed.
If the job restarts, it resumes from the last committed checkpoint. Duplicate candidates are deduplicated downstream on `(cart_id, window_end)`.

commands.cmd: kubectl -n lifecycle logs -l app=recovery-job --since=15m | grep -c 'window_fired'
commands.note: Windows fired in the last 15 minutes — expect 120–180 in peak hours

commands.cmd: flink list -r | grep recovery-abandonment
commands.note: Confirm the job is running and note the job id

commands.cmd: kafka-consumer-groups --describe --group recovery-job
commands.note: Consumer lag; sustained lag over 60 s delays every downstream step

commands.cmd: psql -c "select count(*) from recovery_candidates where created_at > now() - interval '1 hour'"
commands.note: Candidate volume sanity check against the same hour last week

alerts.name: RecoveryJobDown

alerts.name: RecoveryLagHigh
alerts.condition: Consumer lag > 60 s for 5 minutes

alerts.name: CandidateVolumeAnomaly
alerts.condition: Hourly candidates outside ±40% of the trailing 4-week same-hour median

alerts.name: SuppressionMiss
alerts.condition: Any candidate emitted for a customer with a confirmed order in the window

steps.title: Hold for the quiet period
steps.note: 45 minutes — long enough not to be creepy

detail.purpose: Wait long enough that contacting the shopper is helpful rather than unsettling. The number is a judgement about the relationship, not an optimisation target — a shorter window converts marginally better and costs unsubscribes and trust.

outputs.label: Released candidate
outputs.value: Eligible for the recovery decision, or cancelled if activity resumed

runbook: Schedule at `last_activity + 45 minutes`. Any subsequent cart or checkout event cancels the scheduled job outright.
Never send during the shopper's local quiet hours (21:00–08:00). Defer to 08:00 local — a 02:00 nudge is the most reliable way to earn an unsubscribe.
Hold the schedule across deploys; the scheduler is durable and restart-safe by design.
For oversell cancellations the quiet period is zero — the notification is a service message about a specific item, not a marketing nudge.
The 45-minute figure was set by testing 20, 45 and 120 minutes. Twenty converted best and produced 2.4× the unsubscribe rate; 45 was chosen deliberately over the local maximum.

commands.cmd: psql -c "select count(*) from recovery_schedule where fire_at between now() and now() + interval '1 hour'"
commands.note: Upcoming send volume for the next hour

commands.cmd: psql -c "select count(*) from recovery_schedule where fire_at < now() - interval '5 minutes' and fired_at is null"
commands.note: Overdue schedules — should always be zero

commands.cmd: kubectl -n lifecycle rollout status deploy/recovery-scheduler
commands.note: Confirm the scheduler is healthy after a deploy

alerts.name: SchedulerBacklog
alerts.condition: More than 50 schedules overdue by 5 minutes

alerts.name: QuietHoursViolation
alerts.condition: Any send dispatched between 21:00 and 08:00 shopper-local

alerts.name: CancellationRateDrop
alerts.condition: Cancellations below 30% of schedules for an hour — suggests activity events are not arriving

metrics.label: Median actual delay
metrics.value: 45 min · 3 h 20 m including quiet-hour deferrals

steps.title: Is the cart still unconverted?
steps.note: Re-checked at fire time, not at schedule time

detail.purpose: Re-confirm abandonment at the moment of sending rather than trusting a 45-minute-old decision. Emailing someone about a cart they already bought is the single most damaging mistake this pipeline can make.

inputs.label: Live order state
inputs.value: Queried synchronously — never read from a cache

outputs.label: Verdict
outputs.value: `still_abandoned` or `converted`

runbook: Query the order service **synchronously** for any confirmed order by this customer key since the cart was created. Do not trust the event stream at this moment; a lagging consumer becomes an embarrassing email.
Check the cart is still non-empty and still has at least one purchasable line.
On `converted`, close the candidate silently. No email, no log noise, no metric that looks like a failure — it is a success.
On a partially converted cart (some lines ordered, some not), close it. Chasing the remainder reads as surveillance.
If the order service is unavailable, **do not send**. Defer 10 minutes and retry, up to three times, then close the candidate unsent.

alerts.name: SentToConverted
alerts.condition: Any recovery email sent to a customer with a confirmed order in the window

alerts.name: VerdictCheckFailing

alerts.name: ConversionCheckSlow
alerts.condition: p95 verdict latency > 500 ms

branches.label: Already ordered
branches.note: Bought on another device or a second session

exit.label: No contact needed
exit.note: Candidate closed silently — this is a success, not a miss

steps.title: Are we allowed to contact this shopper?
steps.note: Consent, suppression list, frequency cap

detail.purpose: Make the legal and ethical decision before the commercial one. Recovery email is a legitimate-interest communication in most jurisdictions, but only within specific limits, and the limits are the point rather than an obstacle.

inputs.label: Email
inputs.value: Captured at the identify step; absent for many early abandonments

outputs.label: Verdict
outputs.value: `contactable` or `suppressed` with a reason

runbook: No email address means no email. Guests who abandoned before the identify step are unreachable by design, and that is a correct outcome, not a gap to be closed by fingerprinting.
Check the suppression list: unsubscribes, hard bounces, complaint reporters, and anyone in an open support case about this order.
Apply the frequency cap: at most **two** recovery emails per shopper per 30 days, regardless of how many carts they abandon.
Respect the jurisdictional basis. In the EEA/UK recovery mail rides on legitimate interest for existing customers only; a first-time visitor who never ordered requires opt-in.
Log the suppression reason. Suppression counts are a health metric — a sharp fall usually means the consent service is failing open, which is a serious incident.
On any consent-service error, **suppress**. Fail closed on permission, always.

steps.title: Keep the cart warm on site only
steps.note: No email, no ads, no cross-device tricks

detail.purpose: Do the only thing we are entitled to do for an unreachable shopper: keep their cart intact and visible if and when they come back on their own.

outputs.label: Persisted cart
outputs.value: Restored on the next visit from the same browser

outputs.label: Mini-cart badge
outputs.value: Item count visible on return

runbook: Persist the cart against the first-party session cookie for 30 days and restore it silently on the next visit.
Show the item count in the mini-cart badge. That is the entire intervention — no interstitial, no *you left something behind* modal, no countdown.
Do **not** attempt cross-device identity resolution, do not push to an ad audience, and do not fingerprint. A shopper who did not give us an address has told us something and we should listen.
Refresh prices and stock on restore, exactly as the cart screen does for any visit.
Expire the cart at 30 days and delete the snapshot; there is no legitimate reason to hold it longer.

steps.title: Rebuild the cart snapshot for the link
steps.note: Prices and stock refreshed at send time

detail.purpose: Produce an accurate, signed representation of the cart that the recovery email can carry, so the shopper who clicks lands on something true rather than a 45-minute-old fiction.

inputs.label: Live pricing and stock
inputs.value: Fetched at send time, not at detection time

outputs.label: Snapshot
outputs.value: Lines with current price, current availability, and image URLs

outputs.label: Signed link
outputs.value: HMAC token, 7-day expiry, single customer binding

runbook: Re-price and re-check stock now. An email that shows a price the shopper cannot get is worse than no email.
Drop lines that are entirely unavailable and note the drop in the email body — silently shrinking someone's cart in an email is a trust failure.
Render at most three product images. Beyond three the email becomes heavy, clips in Gmail, and converts worse.
Sign the restore link with an HMAC bound to the customer key, with a 7-day expiry. The link restores a cart; it must never restore a *session*.
Store the snapshot so the landing page renders exactly what the email promised, even if stock moves again in between.
If the cart is now empty after the availability pass, close the candidate and send nothing.

steps.title: Send the recovery email
steps.note: One email, no discount, no countdown
steps.destination: Shopper inbox via the transactional ESP

detail.purpose: Send a single useful reminder that makes returning easy. The email's job is to remove friction, not to manufacture urgency — and measurably, the version that does less converts better over the following quarter.

outputs.label: Email
outputs.value: Sent on the transactional stream with a marketing footer

outputs.label: Tracking
outputs.value: Open and click events keyed by candidate id

runbook: Subject line names the item, not the behaviour: `Your Merino crew is still in your cart` — not `You forgot something!`, which reads as a scold.
**No discount.** Discounting abandonment trains shoppers to abandon, and the trained behaviour shows up in margin within two quarters. This is a standing decision, not a per-campaign one.
**No countdown, no fake scarcity.** Real scarcity — a line genuinely down to its last unit — may be stated once, factually.
One primary link, going straight back to the cart with everything restored. No category browsing, no cross-sell grid.
Include the unsubscribe link in the header as well as the footer. Making it easy to leave keeps complaint rates low, and complaint rates are what protect deliverability.
Send on the transactional IP pool but with a marketing footer and full consent metadata; recovery mail is a hybrid and must be treated as the stricter of the two.
Cap at two sends per shopper per 30 days across all campaigns, enforced at dispatch, not at composition.

steps.title: Did the shopper come back within 72 hours?
steps.note: One window, one decision

detail.purpose: Close the loop on the attempt. Either the shopper came back and we get out of the way, or they did not and we stop — because the second and third nudge are where recovery programmes turn into spam.

inputs.label: Click events
inputs.value: Signed-link clicks keyed by candidate id

inputs.label: Orders
inputs.value: Any confirmed order by the customer key in the window

outputs.label: Attribution
outputs.value: `recovered` \| `no_response`

outputs.label: Candidate closure
outputs.value: Terminal either way

runbook: Attribute an order to recovery if it is confirmed within 72 hours of the send **and** the shopper clicked the link. Time-only attribution overstates the programme substantially.
Report click-attributed and view-through numbers separately, always. Blending them is how a recovery programme convinces itself it is twice as valuable as it is.
At most **one** follow-up nudge, at 24 hours, and only for shoppers who clicked but did not order. Someone who did not open twice has answered.
Close the candidate at 72 hours regardless of outcome. There is no third attempt in this system.
Feed the outcome back into the send-time model so the furthest-step signal keeps its weight current.

steps.note: Clickers only — never a second cold email

detail.purpose: Give one more chance to shoppers who showed genuine interest by clicking, without touching anyone who has already declined by silence.

runbook: Only shoppers who **clicked** the first email are eligible. Non-openers are not nudged; silence is an answer.
The nudge must count against the 30-day frequency cap like any other send.
Vary the subject line — repeating the first one gets threaded, collapsed and ignored by most clients.
Re-verify stock before sending. Twenty-four hours is long enough for the cart to have changed materially.
There is no third email. This is enforced in the scheduler, not left to campaign configuration, because campaign configuration always drifts.

steps.title: Close the candidate and stop
steps.note: No third contact, ever

detail.purpose: End the process cleanly, keep the cart available on site, and make sure nothing in the system can decide to try again.

runbook: Mark the candidate `closed_no_response` and write the reason. Terminal states are never reopened by any job.
Leave the cart persisted for 30 days so a shopper who returns on their own finds it intact.
Add the customer key to a 30-day re-entry exclusion so a new abandonment tomorrow does not restart the sequence immediately.
Write the outcome to the analytics warehouse for the weekly review; unrecovered carts are the input to the funnel work, not just a loss.
If the shopper abandoned at the payment step, tag the candidate for the payments team — repeated payment-step abandonment by one shopper is usually a fixable decline problem, not disinterest.

steps.title: Did the cart restore cleanly?
steps.note: Prices and stock re-checked on landing

detail.purpose: Put the returning shopper back exactly where they left off, and be honest the moment that is not possible. A restore that quietly differs from the email is worse than no email at all.

inputs.label: Signed token
inputs.value: HMAC, 7-day expiry, bound to the customer key

outputs.label: Restored cart
outputs.value: In a fresh session, ready for checkout

outputs.label: Drift report
outputs.value: Lines whose price or availability moved since the email

runbook: Verify the HMAC and the expiry first. An expired link lands on the cart page with a plain `This link has expired` and the cart restored anyway where the session allows.
Restore the cart, never the session. A link in an email must not authenticate anybody — that is a account-takeover vector delivered by post.
Diff the snapshot against live prices and stock. Any difference is drift and must be shown.
If nothing changed, land the shopper on the cart with no message at all. Silence is the correct celebration.
If something changed, land on the cart with the changed lines flagged and the totals recomputed — never with the email's stale totals.
Emit `recovery.session_restored` with the drift summary so the programme can see how often it is promising something slightly untrue.

branches.label: Prices or stock changed
branches.note: Say so before they notice it themselves

steps.title: Show exactly what changed since the email
steps.note: Old and new, side by side

detail.purpose: Be the one who points out the difference. A shopper who spots a price change themselves after being emailed about it concludes they were baited; a shopper who is told concludes we are careful.

inputs.label: Drift report
inputs.value: Per line: emailed price, current price, availability

outputs.label: Annotated cart
outputs.value: Changed lines flagged with both values

outputs.label: Honoured price
outputs.value: Where the emailed price was lower and the gap is under £10

runbook: Flag every changed line with the emailed value and the current value, both visible. Never show only the new number.
**Honour the emailed price** where it was lower and the difference is under £10 per line. The goodwill is worth vastly more than the margin, and the alternative is a shopper who feels tricked.
For a line that sold out, say so plainly, offer the nearest alternative, and recompute the total without it.
Keep the shopper on the cart page. Do not push them forward into checkout with a changed order they have not read.
Log every honoured price with the reason so finance can see the cost of the policy — it runs at roughly £340 a week and is reviewed quarterly.
